power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits characterize a severe group of antisocial youth.
Secondary CU traits, distinguished by co-occurring anxiety, are theorized to be acquired when emotionally sensitive children experience prolonged adversity.
We tested this acquired hypothesis from age 10 to 16 in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (baseline N = 11,860, Mage = 9.96, 47.8% female).
Dimensional models in the whole sample regressed CU traits at 16 on baseline emotional sensitivity, cumulative adversity, and their interaction.
Retrospective models tested whether sensitivity and lifetime adversity predicted classification at 16 as secondary CU (anxiety T ≥ 60) rather than primary CU (anxiety T = 50) or anxiety-only.
Prospective models followed sensitive youth (≥ 90th percentile) with no CU traits at age 10 (n = 364).

Contrary to the acquired hypothesis, the sensitivity × adversity interaction on later CU traits was negative (B = -.076, p < .001): adversity predicted later CU traits, but more weakly in more sensitive youth.
text.formatted: Contrary to the acquired hypothesis, the sensitivity × adversity interaction on later CU traits was negative (B = -.076, p < .001): adversity predicted later CU traits, but more weakly in more sensitive youth.

text.text: Sensitivity and adversity did not interact to predict secondary over primary CU (B = .004, family-bootstrap 95% CI: -.11, .21), and in sensitive youth without CU traits, no form of adversity predicted CU traits at 16.
Results held across alternative measures of sensitivity and adversity, anxiety cutoffs, and covariate sets.

Between ages 10 and 16, these data do not support an adversity-driven pathway to CU traits in emotionally sensitive youth; results were consistent instead with comorbid clinical severity or overlapping trait liabilities.
These conclusions, however, do not preclude an acquired pathway operating earlier.
Youth conduct problems pose a significant public health issue.

The youth themselves often face serious downstream consequences, including higher rates of trauma exposure, institutionalization and incarceration, and premature mortality (Fairchild et al., 2019), while also imposing great harm to others (De Brito et al., 2021; Gatner et al., 2023) and substantial economic costs (Gatner et al., 2023; Rivenbark et al., 2018).

text.text: Thus, delivery of the timeliest, most effective interventions for these youth is critical, and the development of such interventions hinges upon a precise, nuanced understanding of the developmental pathways to youth conduct problems.

Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, characterized by deficient empathy, remorse, and affect, and theorized to capture the affective facet of psychopathy in adulthood (Hare & Neumann, 2008), are particularly helpful for designating a distinct pathway to conduct problems and have been codified in diagnostic systems with the Limited Prosocial Emotions (LPE) specifier for conduct disorders (American Psychiatric Association, 2013; World Health Organization, 2019).

text.text: Elevated CU traits distinguish a severe group of antisocial youth who warrant specialized treatment (Frick et al., 2014a (Frick et al., , 2014b)), as these youth often display more harmful and versatile misconduct, including proactive aggression, and are at elevated risk for antisocial personality features in adulthood (De Brito et al., 2021; Frick et al., 2014a Frick et al., , 2014b;; Ritchie et al., 2022).

text.text: One way to enhance therapies for these youth is to better disentangle causal mechanisms.
Deficient empathy development is considered central to the etiology and expression of CU traits (Frick & Kemp, 2021).

text.text: However, like most psychopathological phenomena, CU traits present with multiple forms.

The primary variant (the "prototypical" form) has historically received the most attention, is thought to be largely inherited, and is characterized by emotional, physiological, and neurobiological (e.g., amygdala) hyporeactivity to socioemotional cues along with low trait fearfulness or anxiety (Craig et al., 2021).

text.text: In contrast, the secondary variant is characterized by CU traits that co-occur with high levels of anxiety and hyperreactivity to emotional cues (Craig et al., 2021; Todorov et al., 2025).

text.text: Distinguishable primary and secondary variants have been found across reporter types, levels of analysis, and youth and adult samples (Cassart et al., 2025; Cecil et al., 2018; Craig et al., 2021; Todorov et al., 2025).

text.text: Youth with secondary CU traits are also distinct from anxious-or internalizing-only peers, showing less empathy, greater interpersonal problems, and more aversive parenting (Cassart et al., 2025); across comparisons, they often show the worst behavioral outcomes, including higher aggression (Craig et al., 2021).

text.text: This clinically severe profile raises questions about its development.

Whether anxiety-defined primary and secondary groups represent distinct developmental phenotypes, rather than differences in broader internalizing problems, measurement, or symptom configuration, remains an open question, particularly in community samples and at younger ages.
Nor is it clear why CU traits and anxiety co-occur.
There are three main hypotheses.

The first comes from the psychopathy literature and Karpman (1941), who described primary psychopathy as inborn while the secondary form was theorized to be acquired in response to environmental stress.

text.text: For instance, Kimonis (2023) developed the Emotionally Sensitive Child-Adverse Parenting Experiences-Allostatic Load (ESCAPE-AL) model, which proposes that children with high trait emotional sensitivity who experience prolonged adversity develop CU traits as a defense mechanism (i.e., emotional/empathic numbing) to regulate overwhelming distress.

text.text: In this acquired hypothesis, the secondary variant presents a kind of acquired "phenocopy" of primary CU in which a "callous façade" develops over time as a maladaptive trauma response leading to troubling consequences like conduct problems.
Though the acquired hypothesis remains dominant, it is important to acknowledge alternatives.
One holds that co-occurring anxiety is a consequence of more severe behavior, flipping the directionality of symptoms.

For example, Robertson et al. (2023) found that in high-CU youth, higher aggression predicted later increases in anxiety, suggesting co-occurring anxiety marks behavioral severity rather than an independent pathway.

text.text: Here, behavior is the link between CU traits and later anxiety: aggression and risk-taking raise exposure to victimization and trauma, which may in turn precipitate anxiety, plausible given that secondary CU traits co-occur with both greater trauma histories and more severe, wide-ranging behavior problems (Craig et al., 2021).

text.text: A third possibility is a dual-risk or overlapping liability hypothesis.

Children may inherit broad risk factors that predispose them simultaneously to elevations on both CU traits and internalizing problems marked by anxiety, heightened emotional reactivity, or negative affect.

In this view, the secondary variant is not adversity-driven, and neither anxiety nor CU traits follow the other; rather, it reflects the co-occurrence of two trait liabilities that may have been present from the start.
These hypotheses, acquired, behavioral consequence, and dual-liability, are not mutually exclusive, and none has been established as definitive (Frick & Dickens, 2006; Robertson et al., 2023).

text.text: We focus on the acquired hypothesis because it remains the prevailing framework and, if correct, carries distinct clinical implications: it would prioritize screening for and treating emotional sensitivity and adversity exposure (e.g., via emotion-regulation or trauma-focused intervention), in contrast to existing CU-specific modifications that target deficient emotional reactivity and prosocial behavior (Fleming et al., 2022; Kimonis et al., 2019).

text.text: This study used both retrospective and prospective analyses to test the acquired hypothesis for secondary CU traits.
Using the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, a large, epidemiologically informed longitudinal cohort, we tested the acquired hypothesis from age 10 to age 16 in three ways.

First, dimensional tests in the whole sample asked whether baseline emotional sensitivity and cumulative adversity interact to predict CU traits at 16; the acquired hypothesis predicts that adversity raises CU traits more in sensitive youth.

Second, retrospective tests used the cutoffs applied in prior work, which we treat as that literature's operationalization rather than as validated subtypes, to distinguish primary CU (elevated CU traits, no co-occurring anxiety), secondary CU (elevated CU traits with elevated anxiety) and anxiety-only presentations at 16, and asked whether baseline sensitivity and lifetime adversity interact to predict secondary over primary CU.
Third, prospective tests followed highly sensitive youth with no CU traits at baseline and asked whether cumulative adversity predicted the increase or onset of CU traits.

Importantly, we do not assume adolescence is the primary etiological period for CU traits but treat it as a theoretically informative window in which socioemotional systems, adversity exposure, and regulatory demands expand and reorganize (Pollmann et al., 2025; Steinberg, 2014).

text.text: If CU traits can be acquired through prolonged adversity in emotionally sensitive youth, adolescence should be a detectable period for such processes; null findings would suggest the pathway operates earlier, is confined to more severe clinical contexts, or is less central than theorized.

Analyses tested the acquired hypothesis for secondary CU traits in three complementary ways.
Dimensional analyses in the whole sample asked whether baseline emotional sensitivity and cumulative adversity interact to predict CU traits at age 16.

Retrospective analyses asked whether baseline sensitivity and lifetime adversity predicted later classification as having secondary CU traits, relative to primary CU traits or an anxiety-only presentation.
Prospective analyses asked whether emotionally sensitive youth with no CU traits at baseline developed CU traits following cumulative adversity exposure.

CU traits at age 16 (summed score) were regressed on baseline emotional sensitivity, cumulative adversity (unit-weighted composite), their interaction, and the covariates, using linear regression with family-clustered standard errors; negative binomial models were fit as a check on the count outcome.

Per the acquired pathway, we predicted a positive interaction: adversity should raise later CU traits more in sensitive youth.

In sum, no operationalization of sensitivity or adversity produced the positive sensitivity × adversity interaction on later CU traits that the acquired hypothesis predicts, whether looking backward from age 16 or forward from age 10.
Can CU traits be acquired through adversity in emotionally sensitive youth?

We tested this from age 10 to age 16 in the full ABCD cohort, with dimensional, retrospective, and prospective designs and with several theoretically and empirically driven operationalizations of sensitivity and adversity.
Within that window we found no support for it.
In the whole sample, adversity predicted later CU traits across the probed range of sensitivity, but less strongly for more highly sensitive youth, the opposite of the acquired prediction.
Sensitivity and adversity did not interact to predict who was classified as secondary rather than primary CU at 16.
Sensitive youth who had no CU traits at age 10 did not acquire them in proportion to the adversity they experienced.
These conclusions held under alternative sensitivity measures, adversity indices, anxiety cutoffs and covariate sets, and with family-clustered inference.

This pattern converges with longitudinal community evidence from earlier in development, using a comparable anxiety-based classification: in the ELISA cohort, with temperament and parenting measured at age 4 and variants classified from ages 5 to 10, early environmental risk did not selectively predict secondary CU; punitive parenting and lower parental warmth predicted both variants, whereas fearlessness uniquely predicted the primary variant (Álvarez-Voces et al., 2026).

text.text: The dimensional finding deserves a plain statement.
Adversity was associated with higher CU traits at 16, by about 0.1 to 0.2 points per SD.
That association was attenuated, not reversed, in sensitive youth.

One reading is that emotionally sensitive children respond to adversity with the anxiety and dysphoria the sensitivity composite indexes, rather than with the callousness the acquired model proposes, so that adversity's association with CU traits is carried by less reactive youth.

We note the alternative that the composite, built from parent-reported symptoms, is a poor index of the temperament the model has in mind; the results with the EATQ-R and the youth-reported BIS were weaker but in no case in the predicted direction.
Our findings are more consistent with the dual-risk or overlapping liability hypothesis.

Youth classified as secondary CU at 16 were already the most impaired group at age 10 on every symptom measure: CU traits equal to those of primary youth, and higher anxiety, depression, irritability, and aggression than both comparison groups.

The retrospective models adjust for these baseline levels, so they test whether sensitivity and adversity predict the group difference that arises between ages 10 and 16, among youth comparable at 10; within that window they do not.
The same ordering held at age 16, where secondary youth were the only group whose aggression rose over the follow-up.

Results in the sensitive no-CU group are also consistent: neither adversity nor baseline aggression predicted later CU traits, and family history of antisocial behavior was the only consistent predictor.

These profiles are compatible with co-occurring heritable or temperamental risk (Tomlinson et al., 2026) and with an acquired pathway that was complete before age 10; they do not distinguish between them.

text.text: Neither the dual-liability nor the behavioral-consequence account (Robertson et al., 2023) was tested here.

text.text: Testing the consequence account requires repeated measures of CU traits, behavior, exposure and anxiety and models that separate within-person change from stable differences.
This design tests the acquired pathway between ages 10 and 16.
Because every model adjusts for, or selects on, CU traits at age 10, it cannot detect a process completed earlier in childhood, and we do not claim otherwise.

Adolescence is nonetheless a period in which the acquired account makes predictions: exposure to adversity outside the family increases, CU traits are commonly assessed in clinical and justice settings at these ages, and most of the evidence for secondary variants comes from adolescent samples (Craig et al., 2021).

text.text: Our sample carried the exposure the hypothesis requires, with a tenth of parents reporting four or more negative life events and a tenth of youth five or more by age 15, and higher rates in the sensitive subsample.
If sensitive youth can acquire CU traits through adversity in this period, that process should have been observable here, and it was not.

It remains possible that the acquired hypothesis, as proposed in ESCAPE-AL (Kimonis, 2023), applies to earlier childhood, to the most severe clinical populations, or to particular forms of adversity, such as sexual abuse, that this study could not capture (McLaughlin & Gabard-Durnam, 2022).

text.text: Testing it there will require cohorts followed from early childhood with temperament measured before CU traits emerge.
The cutoff-defined groups should be read as the operationalization used in prior work, not as validated subtypes.

In this cohort, 44% of youth with elevated CU traits at 16 fell between the primary and secondary anxiety cutoffs and were classified by neither, and classifying them as primary did not change the conclusions.

Identifying which features, such as anxiety, emotional reactivity, trauma exposure, and their timing, mark a distinct secondary variant is a precondition for testing developmental models of how such a variant arises, and the present results suggest that this work is not finished.
Several limitations should be considered.

All measures were parent-reported except where noted, and the same parent reported CU traits, anxiety, and aggression, so shared method contributes to their associations; future work should incorporate multi-method indices of emotional sensitivity, anxiety, and CU traits.

The CU measure is brief and parent-reported: four items, three of them reverse-scored prosocial items, validated in this cohort (Hawes et al., 2020) and the only CU measure available for the full sample at every wave, but it does not cover the full content of established instruments and has a marked floor ( 53to 59% of youth score zero at each wave).

text.text: Models using lifetime adversity lost about 30% of cases listwise because life events were first assessed at the 1-year follow-up, more among primary youth, and retained youth had somewhat more PTEs and higher sensitivity than excluded youth.

Finally, ABCD is a community cohort, and the pathway may operate only in the more severe clinical or justice-involved contexts in which secondary variants have mostly been described; replication in clinic-referred or justiceinvolved samples is warranted.
The findings bear on clinical research rather than on practice, because observational associations between adversity and symptom change do not estimate treatment effects.

They suggest that, at least in this period, reducing adversity exposure alone would not be expected to prevent secondary CU traits, and that trials comparing trauma-focused components with approaches that address co-occurring CU traits and anxiety directly, such as emotion regulation and anxiety management (Linehan, 2020) alongside coaching empathic and prosocial skills, would be informative for youth presenting with both.

text.text: In conclusion, between ages 10 and 16 in a large community cohort, we found no support for an adversity-driven pathway to CU traits in emotionally sensitive youth.
Adversity predicted later CU traits, but less so in the most sensitive.
Youth with secondary CU traits were already the most impaired at age 10, consistent with pre-existing temperamental and/or genetic liabilities.
The acquired account may yet hold for earlier childhood or for more severe populations, but in the window these data observe it did not.
Disentangling these mechanisms remains crucial for improving prevention and treatment for antisocial youth with CU and anxiety features.
